title: Capstone Compare
bigQuestion: How can two sword sports, Olympic fencing and kendo, be compared by origin, room, nation and code using dated records?

story.title: Two Rule Books, One Page Each
story.kicker: Two rule books open to the page that says who may step forward and begin.
paragraphs: On a library table lie two rule books. One is the rule book of the International Fencing Federation, known by its French initials, FIE. The other is a set of kendo match regulations from the International Kendo Federation. A student has opened each to the page that names who may compete.

The fencing page says a fencer must hold a licence from the FIE, issued through a national federation. It also lists the commands a referee gives in French to begin a bout. The kendo page describes three referees, each holding a red flag and a white flag, and the command that starts a match.

Both sports use a blade that cannot cut. Both began in rooms where people once trained for real sword fights. Yet one became part of every modern Olympic Games, and the other has never been on the Olympic program.

A fair comparison sets these facts side by side with their dates. It asks where each sport began, what rooms it used, which nations shaped it, and which bodies wrote its code. It does not ask which sword sport is better.
story.think: What can the first page of a rule book tell you about the body that wrote it?

lessons.title: Masters of Arms in Paris
lessons.mainIdea: Fencing masters in Paris received a royal charter in 1567, and their salles turned sword training into a taught, regulated craft.
reading: In 1567 King Charles IX of France granted letters patent to the fencing masters of Paris. *Letters patent* are an open royal document that grants a right or a status. The charter let the masters govern their own trade, test new teachers and control who could teach. A master of arms had to pass through years as a pupil and assistant.

Training took place in a *salle d'armes*, a hall of arms. In the 1600s and 1700s, gentlemen carried a light thrusting sword called the smallsword. French masters developed a lighter training weapon, the foil, with a blunted tip. They also wrote conventions about which fencer had the right to score first.

Those conventions later became the rules of foil fencing. The salle was both a school and a social club for men of the upper classes. Women and working people were mostly shut out of it for centuries. The French words used in the salle, such as en garde, stayed in fencing everywhere.

words.d: an open royal document granting a right or status, such as the 1567 charter to Paris fencing masters
a hall of arms; a fencing school
a light fencing weapon with a blunted tip, first made for training

look.title: A Guild Sets the Door
look.text: Paris, late 1500s. A young man wants to teach fencing for money. The masters' charter says he must first serve as a pupil, then an assistant, and then pass a test before the masters. Anyone teaching without their approval can be stopped.
look.prompt: How did the 1567 charter decide who could teach fencing, and whom might it leave out?

check.q: Who granted the Paris fencing masters their charter in 1567?
check.why: King Charles IX granted letters patent to the Paris masters in 1567.

check.q: What is a salle d'armes?
choices: A fencing school or hall of arms
check.why: Salle d'armes means hall of arms, a fencing school.

check.q: Why was the foil first made?
check.why: French masters developed the blunted foil as a light training weapon.

lessons.title: Sword Halls in Edo
lessons.mainIdea: In the 1800s, large sword halls in Edo taught thousands of students with bamboo swords, creating the rooms that later became kendo.
reading: Edo, now Tokyo, was the seat of the Tokugawa shoguns from 1603 to 1868. By the early 1800s the city had many sword *dojo*, training halls tied to a named school. Three became famous as the great halls of Edo. They belonged to the Hokushin Ittō-ryū, the Shintō Munen-ryū and the Kyōshin Meichi-ryū.

Chiba Shūsaku founded the Hokushin Ittō-ryū and opened his Genbukan hall in Edo in the 1820s. His hall trained with shinai and armor and drew many students. Students were mostly from samurai families, though some commoners also trained. Young men from many domains came to the capital to study at these halls.

A dojo of this kind had a named *school*, or ryū, a founder, and licenses that recorded a student's progress. That makes it similar to the Paris salle, with its guild and masters. Both were private teaching rooms, and both ruled who could teach. Neither was yet a national sport body.

words.d: a training hall; in the Edo period, one tied to a named sword school
a Japanese school or tradition of an art, with a founder and a line of teachers
the old name of Tokyo, seat of the Tokugawa shoguns from 1603 to 1868

look.title: Salle and Dojo Side by Side
look.text: Paris salle, 1700s: a master licensed by a guild, pupils from the upper classes, a blunted foil. Edo dojo, 1820s: a founder of a named school, pupils mostly from samurai families, a bamboo shinai. Each room keeps its own records of who may teach.
look.prompt: Name two ways these rooms were alike and one way they differed.

check.q: What was Edo?
check.why: Edo was the old name of Tokyo, the Tokugawa capital.

check.q: Who founded the Hokushin Ittō-ryū?
check.why: Chiba Shūsaku founded the Hokushin Ittō-ryū and its Genbukan hall.

check.q: What is a ryū?
choices: A school or tradition with a founder and a line of teachers
check.why: A ryū is a Japanese school of an art with a founder and teaching line.

lessons.title: When Swords Left Daily Life
lessons.mainIdea: Japan banned wearing swords in public in 1876, while France allowed dueling far longer, and both changes pushed sword arts toward sport.
reading: In 1876 the Meiji government issued the *Haitōrei*, an order that banned most people from wearing swords in public. The samurai class had already lost its legal privileges. Sword teachers lost pupils and income. Some staged public gekiken shows with paid tickets to earn a living.

In France, the sword stayed in public life longer through the *duel*, a private fight arranged to settle a question of honor. Duels were illegal in theory but often tolerated. The épée, a heavier thrusting sword used in duels, became a sport weapon in the late 1800s. The last widely reported duel in France took place in 1967, between two politicians, Gaston Defferre and René Ribière.

In both countries the real sword faded from daily life over the same broad period. Sword training then needed a new reason to exist. In Japan the new reason was national education and budo. In France it was sport, clubs and international contests, including the Olympic Games from 1896.

words.d: the 1876 Japanese order that banned most people from wearing swords in public
a private fight arranged to settle a question of honor
a heavier fencing sword based on the dueling sword

check.why: The 1876 order banned most people from wearing swords in public.

check.q: What is a duel?
choices: A private fight to settle a question of honor
check.why: A duel is a private fight arranged to settle a question of honor.

check.q: Which sport weapon grew from the dueling sword?
check.why: The épée, a heavier thrusting sword, is based on the dueling sword.

lessons.title: The FIE, Paris 1913
lessons.mainIdea: The International Fencing Federation was founded in Paris in 1913, and French remains the language of fencing's commands.
reading: Fencing was on the program of the first modern Olympic Games at Athens in 1896. It is one of only a few sports held at every modern Games. At first each country and each tournament used its own rules. Disputes over judging were common, because a touch was hard to see and judges often disagreed.

In 1913 national federations met in Paris and founded the *Fédération Internationale d'Escrime*, the FIE. An *international federation* is a body that writes one set of rules for a sport across countries. The FIE took over the rules for foil, épée and sabre. Today its headquarters are in Lausanne, Switzerland, the city that also hosts the International Olympic Committee.

The FIE rules give referee commands in French. A referee says en garde, then prêts, then allez to begin, and halte to stop. A fencer in Tokyo or Chicago hears the same French words. Language in a rule book keeps a record of where a sport's code was first written.

words.d: Fédération Internationale d'Escrime; the International Fencing Federation, founded in Paris in 1913
a body that writes one set of rules for a sport across many countries
the French command a fencing referee gives to set fencers ready

check.why: National federations founded the FIE in Paris in 1913.

check.q: What language do FIE referee commands use?
check.why: FIE rules give referee commands in French, such as en garde and allez.

check.q: What does an international federation do?
choices: Writes one set of rules for a sport across countries
check.why: An international federation writes common rules across many countries.

lessons.title: Kendo Federations, 1952 and 1970
lessons.mainIdea: Kendo gained a national federation in 1952 and an international one in 1970, which held the first World Kendo Championships that year.
reading: The All Japan Kendo Federation was founded in 1952, after the Allied occupation of Japan ended. It wrote national rules and ran grading examinations. In the United States, Japanese American clubs had practiced kendo since before the Second World War. Clubs also grew in Brazil, Korea, Taiwan and Europe.

In 1970 national and regional kendo federations founded the International Kendo Federation, known as the *FIK*. That same year the FIK held the first World Kendo Championships in Tokyo. The world championships have been held every three years since then, in cities from São Paulo to Paris.

Kendo is not an Olympic sport. Many kendo leaders have argued that Olympic entry would push the art toward winning and away from its educational aims. That argument is a choice about the room kendo wants. Fencing made the opposite choice in 1896 and stayed with it.

words.d: the International Kendo Federation, founded in 1970
international kendo contests held every three years since 1970
the national body for kendo in Japan, founded in 1952

look.title: Two Answers to One Invitation
look.text: Fencing, 1896: on the program in Athens and never left. Kendo, 1970 onward: world championships every three years, but no Olympic event. Both have world bodies, rule books and ranked referees.
look.prompt: Why might two sports with world federations make different choices about the Olympic Games?

check.q: When was the All Japan Kendo Federation founded?
check.why: The All Japan Kendo Federation was founded in 1952.

check.q: Where were the first World Kendo Championships held?
check.why: The FIK held the first World Kendo Championships in Tokyo in 1970.

check.q: What reason have many kendo leaders given for staying out of the Olympics?
choices: It could push the art toward winning and away from education
check.why: Many kendo leaders argue Olympic entry would shift kendo toward winning over its educational aims.

lessons.title: Wire Versus Flags
lessons.mainIdea: Fencing adopted electric scoring for épée at the 1936 Olympics, while kendo still relies on three referees with flags.
reading: At the 1936 Olympic Games in Berlin, épée bouts were scored with *electric scoring* for the first time. A wire connected each fencer's weapon to a box that lit a lamp when a touch landed. Foil followed at the 1956 Games in Melbourne. Sabre was the last weapon to go electric, in the late 1980s.

Kendo took a different path. A kendo match has three *shinpan*, or referees, each holding a red flag and a white flag. A point, called ippon, counts when at least two referees raise their flags for the same competitor. The referees judge not only contact but also form, spirit and posture, following the federation's rules.

The two systems record different ideas of what a point is. Fencing's machine answers whether a touch landed, and a referee applies the right-of-way conventions in foil and sabre. Kendo's panel asks whether a strike met the federation's full standard. Neither system is more modern in a ranking sense; each fits its own code.

words.d: a system in which a wired weapon lights a lamp when a touch lands; first used for Olympic épée in 1936
a kendo referee; a match has three, each with a red and a white flag
in kendo, a point awarded when at least two of three referees raise their flags

look.title: A Lamp and Two Flags
look.text: In a fencing hall, a red lamp lights on a scoring box, and the referee announces the touch. In a kendo hall, three referees stand at the edges of the court. Two raise white flags; one crosses his flags low to show no point. The point goes to white.
look.prompt: What does each scene show about who or what decides a point?

check.q: Which weapon was first scored electrically at the Olympics, in 1936?
check.why: Épée used electric scoring at the 1936 Berlin Games.

check.q: How many shinpan judge a kendo match?
check.why: A kendo match has three referees, each with a red and a white flag.

check.q: When does ippon count in kendo?
choices: When at least two referees raise flags for the same side
check.why: Ippon counts when at least two of three shinpan raise flags for one competitor.

lessons.title: A Licence to Enter
lessons.mainIdea: To enter FIE competitions, a fencer must hold an FIE licence issued through a national federation, a paper gate that ties each fencer to a nation.
reading: The FIE requires every fencer in its official events to hold an FIE *licence*. A licence is a paper or digital permit that shows a person may take part. Fencers get it through their national federation, which the FIE recognizes. Without one, a fencer cannot start in a World Cup or world championship bout.

This rule ties each fencer to a nation. In the United States, the national body began as the Amateur Fencers League of America in 1891. It is now called USA Fencing. National bodies choose teams, and those teams represent their countries at the Olympic Games.

The licence gives the FIE a list of who fenced, where and for which nation. That list is a historian's record. It shows when new countries joined, when fencers changed nations, and when events opened. It also shows the gate: only those accepted by a national body may begin.

words.d: a permit showing that a person may take part; FIE events require one
the body that runs a sport in one country and is recognized by the world body
the national fencing body of the United States, founded in 1891 as the Amateur Fencers League of America

look.text: A fencer from Chicago wins a regional tournament and wants to enter a World Cup event abroad. The entry form asks for an FIE licence number. She must first be registered with USA Fencing and entered by it.
look.prompt: What steps stand between a strong local fencer and a world event, and who controls each step?

check.q: What must a fencer hold to enter FIE official events?
check.why: The FIE requires a licence for every fencer in its official events.

check.q: Through which body does a fencer get an FIE licence?
check.why: Fencers get the licence through their national federation.

check.q: What was USA Fencing called when it was founded in 1891?
choices: The Amateur Fencers League of America
check.why: USA Fencing began as the Amateur Fencers League of America in 1891.

lessons.title: A Grade Exam to Rise
lessons.mainIdea: In kendo, the national federation ranks practitioners through dan examinations up to eighth dan, which very few candidates pass in any year.
reading: The All Japan Kendo Federation runs *dan* examinations. A dan is a numbered black-belt-level grade; kendo uses the word even though kendo gear has no colored belt. Grades by examination run from first dan to eighth dan. Each higher exam requires a set number of years at the grade below.

The eighth dan examination is known in Japan as one of the hardest tests in any martial art. Candidates must have held seventh dan for many years. Very few pass in any year, and many try again and again. Panels of senior examiners judge the candidates' matches.

The grade system decides who may judge, teach and examine others, not who may enter a first match. A beginner can join a kendo club and compete in local events. In fencing, results and national rankings open doors; in kendo, examined grades carry much of the authority. Each sport answers the question of standing in its own way.

words.d: a numbered advanced grade in Japanese arts; kendo grants first to eighth dan by examination
a formal test before a panel that decides whether a person earns a grade
a person's recognized place in a sport, shown by results or grades

look.title: Two Kinds of Standing
look.text: A fencer's standing is shown by a national ranking list built from tournament results. A kendo teacher's standing is shown by a certificate stating seventh dan, passed before a panel on a given date. Both are written records kept by a federation.
look.prompt: What does each record measure, and why might each sport prefer its own kind?

check.why: The All Japan Kendo Federation runs the dan examinations.

check.q: What is the highest dan awarded by examination in kendo?
check.why: Grades by examination run from first to eighth dan.

check.q: What does a kendo grade mainly decide, according to the reading?
choices: Who may judge, teach and examine others
Who may enter a first local match
check.why: The grade decides who may judge, teach and examine; beginners can still join and compete.

lessons.title: Wheelchair Fencing, Rome 1960
lessons.mainIdea: Wheelchair fencing was part of the first Paralympic Games in Rome in 1960, opening fencing's starting line to athletes with disabilities.
reading: In 1948 the doctor Ludwig Guttmann held a sports competition for injured military veterans at Stoke Mandeville Hospital in England. Many of them used wheelchairs after spinal injuries in the Second World War. Guttmann believed sport helped patients recover strength and confidence. His games grew each year.

In 1960 the event was held in Rome after the Olympic Games, and it is now counted as the first *Paralympic Games*. *Wheelchair fencing* was on its program. The wheelchairs are fixed to a frame on the floor, so fencers face each other at a set distance. Fencers use the same three weapons as in Olympic fencing.

Wheelchair fencing has been held at every Summer Paralympics since 1960. The rule of the fixed frame answered a practical question about who may start: it let athletes who use wheelchairs compete on equal terms. The event shows how a code can be rewritten to open a door, rather than keep one shut.

words.d: the international games for athletes with disabilities; the first counted Games were held in Rome in 1960
fencing in wheelchairs fixed to a floor frame; part of every Summer Paralympics since 1960
a doctor who began games for injured veterans at Stoke Mandeville, England, in 1948

check.q: When was wheelchair fencing first on the Paralympic program?
check.why: Wheelchair fencing was part of the first Paralympic Games in Rome in 1960.

lessons.title: A Second Pair: Sumo and Schwingen
lessons.mainIdea: Japan's sumo and Switzerland's schwingen are both national wrestling traditions with their own bodies, rings and rules, so they can be compared by date.
reading: Professional sumo in Japan is run by the Japan Sumo Association. Its forerunner was formed in 1925 by joining the Tokyo and Osaka groups. Since 1958 it has held six grand tournaments a year. The association sets entry rules for new wrestlers, and since 2002 it has limited each training stable to one foreign-born wrestler.

*Schwingen* is Swiss wrestling, held in a ring covered with sawdust. Wrestlers wear short canvas trousers over their clothes. The Federal Wrestling Association, the Eidgenössischer Schwingerverband, was founded in 1895. Its biggest festival is held every three years, and the champion is traditionally given a bull as a prize.

The two can be compared with the same questions used for fencing and kendo. Sumo is professional; schwingen wrestlers are amateurs who win prizes in kind, such as livestock, not salaries. Sumo's home is a national arena; schwingen's is an outdoor festival. Each is a *national tradition*, and each body decides who may enter its ring.

words.d: Swiss wrestling held in a sawdust ring, organized by a federal association founded in 1895
in sumo, a training house where wrestlers live and practice under a stablemaster
a practice a country treats as part of its shared identity

lessons.title: Comparing Without a Winner
lessons.mainIdea: A strong comparison sets dated facts about origin, room, nation and code side by side and explains differences without ranking the arts.
reading: Historians of sport use *comparison* to see what is shared and what is particular. For fencing and kendo, the origin question has dated answers: the Paris charter of 1567 and the Edo halls of the early 1800s. The room question has answers too: the salle and the dojo. Each can be checked in records.

The nation question asks which states shaped each art. France gave fencing its words and its world body in 1913. Japan gave kendo its name, its national federation in 1952 and a place in school physical education. The code question asks who writes the rules: the FIE for fencing, the FIK and national federations for kendo.

A comparison becomes a *ranking* when it treats one set of answers as the standard. Calling kendo less modern because it uses flags, or fencing less serious because it uses a machine, adds a judgment the records do not support. The dated evidence shows two institutions that made different choices, each with its own reasons.

words.d: setting two things side by side to see what is shared and what is particular
ordering things from better to worse by one standard
records and facts that support a claim
